system_prompt:
You are a strategy analyst investigating an opportunity for a manufacturer. Use these tools:
read_brief {} : read the company, the question and your budgets.
frame_problem {"objective":"...","constraints":["..."],"alternatives":["..."]} : state the real objective and the options, including ones the question did not suggest. Accepted once.
search_evidence {"query":"..."} : keyword search of the evidence. Uses one search.
challenge_theory {"theory_id":"T1","query":"..."} : search for evidence that could prove a theory wrong. Uses one search.
read_source {"id":"..."} : read a result found by search.
add_theory {"claim":"...","who_benefits":"...","why_behaviour_changes":"...","how_value_is_captured":"...","assumptions":["..."],"predictions":["..."]} : add one causal theory of value. Returns its id.
assess_evidence {"theory_id":"T1","evidence_id":"...","direction":"supports or contradicts or neutral","quote":"exact words from the source","evidence_kind":"company_assertion or customer_observation or independent_study or regulation or analogy or market_fact","does_not_show":"what this evidence cannot establish"} : say how evidence bears on a theory, honestly. Use neutral if it does neither.
propose_test {"name":"...","theories":["T1","T2"],"method":"...","sample":"...","measure":"...","prediction_by_theory":{"T1":"...","T2":"..."},"decision_rule":"...","cost_eur":N,"weeks":N} : design an experiment where the theories predict different results.
revise_theory {"theory_id":"T1","status":"kept or revised or rejected","reason":"...","new_claim":"the changed claim, or none","evidence_ids":["..."]} : update a theory after new evidence.
finish {"recommendation":"...","target_customer":"...","value_proposition":"...","favoured_theory":"T1","next_action":"...","uncertainty":"...","would_change_if":["..."],"evidence_ids":["..."]} : end the investigation.

Reply with one JSON object: {"name": "<tool>", "arguments": {...}}. A user turn that starts with "Tool result:" is the output of your call. End by calling finish.

Work like a scientist, not a consultant.
1. read_brief, then frame_problem. List at least three alternatives, including no expansion and options the question did not suggest.
2. Search before you theorise. Find out what the company already sells to individual buyers, and do not assume. Read at least three sources.
3. add_theory at least twice, and a third time if you have a different cause. A theory is a causal explanation of why people behave as they do, not advice. Do not write "the company should". Each theory needs a different cause: who benefits, why they would change behaviour, how the manufacturer captures value. Give assumptions, and predictions someone could measure.
For example, from eyewear: "People treat glasses as a medical necessity. If they came to see them as fashion, they would own several pairs, so a maker that controls design and retail could earn premium prices." A rival theory would name a different cause.
4. assess_evidence for every theory, quoting the source's exact words. Say what kind of evidence it is and what it cannot show. A company's own claim is not proof of demand. Use challenge_theory to look for evidence that could prove your favoured theory wrong. If you find nothing against it, say so. Never force a contradiction.
5. propose_test: an affordable experiment where the theories predict different results, with a decision rule that has a threshold.
6. If new evidence arrives, read it and use revise_theory.
7. finish. Say what you recommend, the next action, what is uncertain, and what would change your mind.

Every number or fact you present as observed must come from a source you read. Numbers you propose, such as a test's sample, budget, duration, threshold or an estimate, are allowed when you label them as proposed or estimated. Your theories are hypotheses, not facts. Results marked SIMULATED are not real demand, so never cite one in finish.

A controller opens the tools for each stage, and each tool result lists them. Before you finish you will also use:
decline_test {"reason":"..."} : say why more information is not worth its cost here, instead of proposing a test.
state_position {"favoured_theory":"T1","recommendation":"...","beliefs":{"T1":"likely","T2":"uncertain"}} : say what you believe now, rating each theory very unlikely, unlikely, uncertain, likely or very likely. finish then also takes "beliefs".
A SIMULATED result is a what-if exercise. Reason as if it were real, and say what it would mean for your theories. A result can change nothing. Still keep it out of the evidence you cite.
runtime: Anthropic API, effort medium, no seed or temperature, so runs do not repeat exactly

frame.objective: Decide whether Simonelli Group should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its professional espresso equipment, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. The objective is to learn whether a consumer value capture exists, not to assume one.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or internal data
Company financials may be incomplete, so gaps must be stated rather than filled
Test budget assumed at 20000 EUR and 12 weeks; these are exercise assumptions, not company figures
Eight searches total; seven remaining after the brief
Must separate company claims from independent evidence and observed facts from estimates
alternatives: No expansion: remain a professional-only espresso equipment maker
Consumer home machine under the existing brand, sold through current retail or online channels
Prosumer or home-barista line: premium-design product for enthusiasts, possibly a redesign of a commercial component
Route-to-buyer change: reach consumers via cafes, roasters or subscription coffee-service partners

T1.claim: Home-espresso enthusiasts will pay a premium for commercial-grade components (group heads, boilers, pumps) packaged in a compact, well-designed machine, so a maker with commercial credibility can earn prosumer margins without becoming a mass consumer brand.
T1.who_benefits: Enthusiasts and home-barista buyers who want commercial-grade performance; Simonelli, which would sell a premium line under its existing brand and reuse its component supply chain.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers who already own or aspire to a serious home setup treat machine quality as a visible signal of skill and durability; a commercial-heritage brand signals this more credibly than a generic consumer brand, so they accept a higher price for the same technical content.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Price premium on a prosumer SKU over mass-market home machines, plus reuse of existing component manufacturing so incremental cost is low, and spare-parts or service revenue from a durable installed base.
assumptions: Enthusiast buyers value commercial heritage enough to pay more than for a comparable mass-market machine
Simonelli can sell to home buyers through retail or online channels without a large consumer marketing budget
Component reuse keeps unit costs low enough for a margin at prosumer price points
The prosumer segment is large enough to matter against the company's commercial revenue
predictions: A commercial-heritage home machine priced above comparable mass-market models sells steadily through specialist retailers and online enthusiast channels
Buyers cite build quality, heritage or component specifications rather than price in reviews and surveys
Sales concentrate in enthusiast communities; repeat or accessory purchases (grinders, spares) follow the machine
If buyers instead pick on price or design alone, the premium does not hold and the theory fails
T1.first_claim: Home-espresso enthusiasts will pay a premium for commercial-grade components (group heads, boilers, pumps) packaged in a compact, well-designed machine, so a maker with commercial credibility can earn prosumer margins without becoming a mass consumer brand.

T2.claim: Offices and small lower-volume sites (not expert baristas) buy a compact, low-maintenance commercial-grade espresso machine when it is sold as a managed workplace service, so the value is captured through the placement, servicing and consumables relationship rather than the machine sale alone.
T2.who_benefits: Office managers and small hospitality operators who want café-quality coffee without staff training; Simonelli, which would earn recurring service and consumables revenue and reuse its commercial channel.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Non-expert buyers choose on reliability, ease of use and predictable cost; a service contract removes the risk of breakdown and training, so they accept a recurring fee that a one-off machine purchase would not persuade them to pay.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Recurring service-and-consumables contracts on placed machines, plus the commercial dealer network already used for servicing, rather than a one-off consumer sale.
assumptions: Lower-volume sites will accept a managed service model if uptime and cost predictability are guaranteed
Simonelli's existing dealer and service network can cover distributed small sites economically
The Oscar line's lower-volume positioning already fits this use case
predictions: Small sites adopt a compact machine when the offer includes servicing; uptake falls when it is a bare purchase
Recurring revenue per placed machine exceeds the one-off machine margin over the contract life
Churn is driven by service response times, not by coffee quality

assessments.does_not_show: This is trade-press description of a launch, drawing on the company's own framing. It does not show that enthusiasts pay a premium over mass-market machines, what volumes or margins the Oscar line achieves, or that buyers choose on commercial heritage rather than price or design. It also says nothing about the consumer route to market.

assessments.quote: a colorful new model in its most affordable machine line for homes, offices and other lower-volume environments.
assessments.does_not_show: It shows the company already positions a line for offices and lower-volume sites, which supports that this segment exists in its plans. It does not show that those buyers accept a managed service contract, that recurring service revenue beats one-off machine margin, or how the dealer network would perform across small distributed sites. The service-and-consumables mechanism that defines T2 is untested by this source.

X1.name: Prosumer premium vs managed-office service: price and offer test
X1.method: Two-arm controlled test run in parallel over 12 weeks. Arm A (T1): a commercial-heritage home machine concept shown in enthusiast channels (specialist retailer pages, enthusiast forum ads) at three randomised price points, with a pre-order or refundable deposit. Arm B (T2): an office pilot offering a compact machine at two offers, bare purchase versus purchase with a bundled monthly service-and-consumables contract, placed at a small number of volunteer offices. Both arms use real purchase intent, not stated preference alone.
X1.sample: Arm A: estimated 3,000 to 5,000 unique visitors to enthusiast channels, randomised across three price points. Arm B: estimated 10 to 15 small office or lower-volume sites, split between bare-purchase and service-contract offers. Sample sizes are proposed estimates, not observed figures.
X1.measure: Arm A: deposit conversion rate at each price point and the share of buyers who pick the premium price over the lowest tier. Arm B: take-up of service contract vs bare purchase, and the 8-week renewal intention of contract sites. Both: unit economics estimate of contribution per unit or per contract, using a cost assumption to be confirmed.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Deposit conversion holds or rises at the premium price tier relative to the mass-market reference, and buyers cite build quality or heritage as the reason. Premium tier conversion stays within about 70% of the base tier.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Service-contract offer takes up materially more than bare purchase at comparable sites, and renewal intention is high because uptime and predictable cost matter more than machine price.

X1.decision_rule: Advance T1 to a larger pilot only if premium-tier deposit conversion is at least 70% of the base-tier conversion at the same channel, and at least 20% of enthusiast buyers name heritage or build quality as the main reason. Advance T2 only if at least 40% of pilot sites take the service contract and at least 75% state renewal intent at 8 weeks. If neither threshold is met, decline further spending on either theory. These thresholds are proposed, not evidence-based.

revisions.reason: SYN-SIMO-UPDATE is SIMULATED and is not counted as evidence, so it is not cited here. Real evidence still shows only that the company already sells a prosumer home line (Oscar Mood) and that a rival prosumer brand was acquired for a large sum. Neither shows that enthusiasts pay a premium over mass-market machines. The simulated what-if points to a skill-building mechanism, a candidate sub-theory for later testing, not a reason to change T1. T1's premium claim stays unchanged and untested.

SYN-SIMO-UPDATE is SIMULATED and does not bear on T2, since it concerns an enthusiast skill lesson and no service or office offer. It is not cited. T2 is unchanged: real evidence shows only that offices are a stated target segment for the Oscar line, and nothing yet shows that service contracts beat one-off machine margins. Mechanism remains untested.

As a clearly labelled what-if only: if SYN-SIMO-UPDATE were real, a hands-on skill lesson would raise paid reservations among enthusiasts, suggesting that identity or skill-building drives willingness to pay, which is a candidate sub-mechanism of T1 but not evidence for its premium claim. SIMULATED, not counted in finish, and it does not change T1's status: premium pricing remains untested.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a new consumer proposition yet. Simonelli already sells to home and lower-volume buyers through the Oscar line and the Victoria Arduino Eagle One Prima, so the open question is whether a differentiated premium offer adds value beyond what exists. Run the proposed price-and-offer test (X1) before any product, channel or customer investment. The test is proposed, not run, and its figures are analyst estimates.
final.target_customer: Enthusiast home-espresso buyers (lead hypothesis, T1), with offices and lower-volume sites as a secondary test segment (T2).
final.value_proposition: A commercial-heritage compact machine for enthusiasts, priced above mass-market home machines on build quality and component specification. Unproven on price: no source I read shows a premium.
final.next_action: Run test X1 for up to 12 weeks and about 20000 EUR (both analyst assumptions). Advance T1 only if premium-tier deposit conversion is at least 70% of base-tier conversion and at least 20% of enthusiast buyers cite build quality or heritage. Advance T2 only if at least 40% of pilot sites take the service contract and at least 75% state renewal intent at 8 weeks. First obtain Simonelli's home-line volumes and margins, which I could not find publicly.
final.uncertainty: High. No public source gave home-line sales, margins, pricing or consumer demand. The Oscar Mood article is trade press drawing on company framing. The Breville-Lelit deal is a rival's valuation, not Simonelli's economics. The 2021 Simonelli report is an Italian company claim about product plans only. The challenge surfaced La Marzocco and Victoria Arduino home machines; they do not contradict T1 but do not test it. T2's service mechanism has no supporting source. The simulated SYN-SIMO-UPDATE is not used as evidence.
would_change_if: Disclosed data show home-line revenue is negligible or loss-making
Test X1 shows premium-tier conversion below 70% of base-tier conversion, rejecting T1's premium claim
Buyers in this segment choose on price alone, with no heritage premium
Office pilot shows service-contract take-up below 40% or low renewal intent, rejecting T2
A real study showing a skill-building lesson raises reservations, suggesting a separate mechanism

result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: SYN-SIMO-UPDATE is SIMULATED and is not counted as evidence. As a what-if, it would show that a hands-on home-barista lesson raised paid reservations among enthusiasts, which points to a skill-building or identity mechanism rather than the premium-for-heritage mechanism in T1. It does not test whether enthusiasts pay more for commercial-grade components, so T1's premium claim is unchanged and still untested. If such a mechanism were real, it would be a candidate sub-theory to test later, not a reason to change T1 now. Real evidence on price premium remains absent.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.
